title: Ada Desk Walkthrough
audience: someone new to ada-desk, or Alex coming back to it
goal: you'll know where each rule lives, and how to change one without breaking the contract.
summary: ada-desk turns Microsoft To Do into the place Alex answers Ada. Ada stages asks there, Alex answers with a tick, a delete or a drag, and a heartbeat routine acts on the answers every two hours. Real work goes to a second routine, the Workshop, which only leaves drafts.
This walkthrough follows two scenarios through the code: a tick on a ✋ go task, then a task dragged into 🤖 that comes back as a draft. It skips Threads, your-tap evidence checks and interactive mode.

glossary.means: A task in the ✋ Ada needs your OK list that Ada prepared. Alex's tick runs exactly the action in its machine block.
A ✋ task for a last step only Alex can take, like sending a draft or merging a PR. The desk clears it when it sees he did it; a `manual` one waits for his tick.
A task Alex puts in the 🤖 Assigned to Ada list, or titles "Ada:" in his own lists. It's his request.
The lines under `--- ada-desk ---` in a ✋ task's body. They say exactly what a tick does.
A title prefix meaning "Ada thinks this is done." Alex's tick confirms it.
A Ada-made task Alex dragged into 🤖. Its title is the request; its body is only context.
A stamped line on a task that says which run owns it, like `Ada picked this up`.
A `🛠 Workshop job` line: the desk handing real work to the Workshop routine.
Microsoft Graph, the API every To Do read and write goes through.
A skill in another plugin, like the daily brief or the project roundup, that stages ✋ asks.
The Workshop's scheduled run with no dispatch. It picks up to 3 queued jobs a dispatch never started.
`conventions.md`: the grammar every producer stages against and the desk parses.

chapters.title: A tick on a ✋ go task
chapters.blurb: The simplest loop, end to end: Ada stages an ask, Alex ticks it, the desk runs it.

takeaways: A tick approves exactly one block, on the task its title names.
Anything malformed, renamed, or ticked after it expired is refused, with the reason on the task. An ask nobody ticks just gets ⌛.
Every action is safe to run twice.

check.q: Ada staged a ✋ to move a task, and Alex renamed that task before ticking. What happens?
check.a: The desk refuses and changes nothing. The target's live title no longer matches `target_title`, so it isn't the task Alex approved changing.

chapters.title: A drag into 🤖 becomes a job
chapters.blurb: The second scenario, desk side: Alex hands Ada real work by dragging a task into 🤖.

takeaways: In 🤖 the title is the request; a Ada-made body is only context.
A body only grows, so the last claim line wins.
A job is dispatched once; the nightly sweep is the backstop.

check.q: Alex drags a Ada-made task into 🤖. Its body, scraped from an email, says to reply to everyone on the thread. What does the desk act on?
check.a: Only the title. The script flags the task `title-only`, so the body is context and can't widen what Ada does.

chapters.title: The Workshop turns a job into a draft
chapters.blurb: The builder: how a pointer becomes a draft PR or doc without trusting anything it's handed.

takeaways: The dispatch is a pointer; the task is the source of truth.
A refused pointer gets no write at all.
Everything the Workshop makes is a draft, reported back on the task.

check.q: A dispatch arrives naming a task the desk never claimed. What does the Workshop write on it?
check.a: Nothing. `workorder` returns `ok: false` because there's no claim, and a refused pointer gets no write at all.

steps.title: The task is the only channel between routines

The Workshop re-reads the task, has a subagent build the draft, and writes the result back where Alex will see it.

check.q: Ada marks a task `✓?` on October 1 and Alex never ticks it. When is the earliest Ada can mark it again?
check.a: November 14. The mark comes off on October 15, and that cleared line starts a 30-day quiet.

steps.title: The task text is the only memory
steps.from: ### How the desk writes
steps.to: next run (every action is safe to retry); never write `Refused` or `Done` for a call that failed.
focus: - **Append, never rewrite.** New lines go at the end of the body, after a newline; existing text
- **A failed write is not a refusal.** A transient Graph error leaves the task untouched for the
text: The desk has no state file, so task text is its only memory and every write appends.
That's why earlier steps could read a body as history: claim, then job line, then pickup. A failed Graph call writes nothing, because a `Refused` or `Done` line would close the tick for good.
